Every time a neural network runs, there’s a silent negotiation between
compute and memory.\nIt’s naive to think ML compilers optimize just the
compute - the FLOPs. In reality, they optimize movement. The most
expensive operation in modern compute isn’t your matrix multiply; it’s
getting data from memory to the compute units. This post explores how
layout, tiling, and fusion are the unsung heroes of ML compiler
performance.\n1. The Compiler’s Hidden Battle Deep Learning performance
is a balancing act between compute and memory. You can think of layout
as the grammar of that relationship - the way tensors are arranged,
accessed, and aligned.\nWhether it’s NHWC vs. NCHW, blocked vs. packed,
or interleaved for a Digital Signal Processor (DSP), the layout dictates
cache (scratchpad) reuse and parallelism. During my work on ML
Compilers, I’ve seen how a well-chosen layout can make or break
performance.\n2. Tiling: Breaking Down the Problem Tiling splits large
tensors into smaller, cache-sized tiles. Each tile is small enough to
fit into fast local memory (L1/L2 or SRAM), reducing cache misses and
data movement.\n[ Large Tensor ] | +—–+—–+ | | [ Tile 1 ] [ Tile
2 ] -\u003e split into tiles that fit in cache -\u003e process each
tile independently -\u003e recombine results -\u003e write back to main
memory In MLIR, this concept shows us explicitly:\n%packed = linalg.pack
%input inner_dims_pos = [1, 2] inner_tiles = [8, 8] into
%packed_type The linalg.pack operation materializes a new layout that is
more friendly for the next computation - the compiler’s way of saying
“I’ll arrange the furniture before the guests arrive.”\n3. Fusion:
Keeping Data Hot Once the data is well-tiled, the next goal is to avoid
writing it back.\nThat’s where fusion comes in - combining multiple
operations into one loop nest or kernel so intermediate results stay
“hot” in registers or cache.\nFor example,\n// Unfused version
%matmul_out = linalg.matmul ins(%A, %B : tensor\u003c64x64xf32\u003e,
tensor\u003c64x64xf32\u003e) outs(%tmp : tensor\u003c64x64xf32\u003e)
%relu = linalg.generic { indexing_maps = [ affine_map\u003c(i,j)
-\u003e (i,j)\u003e, // read affine_map\u003c(i,j) -\u003e (i,j)\u003e
// write ], iterator_types = [“parallel”, “parallel”] }
ins(%matmul_out : tensor\u003c64x64xf32\u003e) outs(%result :
tensor\u003c64x64xf32\u003e) { ^bb0(%x: f32, %y: f32): %zero =
arith.constant 0.0 : f32 %max = arith.maxf %x, %zero : f32 linalg.yield
%max : f32 } -\u003e tensor\u003c64x64xf32\u003e // Fused version %fused
= linalg.generic { indexing_maps = [ affine_map\u003c(m,k,n) -\u003e
(m,k)\u003e, // A affine_map\u003c(m,k,n) -\u003e (k,n)\u003e, // B
affine_map\u003c(m,k,n) -\u003e (m,n)\u003e // C ], iterator_types =
[“parallel”, “reduction”, “parallel”] } ins(%A, %B :
tensor\u003c64x64xf32\u003e, tensor\u003c64x64xf32\u003e) outs(%result :
tensor\u003c64x64xf32\u003e) { ^bb0(%a: f32, %b: f32, %c: f32): %prod =
arith.mulf %a, %b : f32 %sum = arith.addf %c, %prod : f32 %zero =
arith.constant 0.0 : f32 %relu = arith.maxf %sum, %zero : f32
linalg.yield %relu : f32 } -\u003e tensor\u003c64x64xf32\u003e Fusing
eliminates the need to write matmul_out back to memory, keeping data in
fast storage and reducing latency. In the fused case, the arith.maxf
(ReLU) happens inside the same loop nest as the accumulation, so %sum
never leaves registers or the cache. No extra kernel launch, no
intermediate writes - just tighter, hotter loops.\n4: The Layout
Tug-of-War Layouts aren’t a one-size-fits-all solution. Different
hardware architectures have different optimal layouts. For
example:\nNHWC favors channels-last access patterns, great for GPUs.
NCHW works better for non-tensor-core accelerators. Blocked layouts
(used on DSPs and NPUs) help vector units process contiguous data
efficiently. Layout propagation passes - such as hoisting or sinking
linalg.pack/linalg.unpack operations - help adapt layouts through the
computation graph, ensuring each operation gets data in its preferred
format.\n5. Case Study: A Small Change, A Big Impact During one
optimization session, I experimented with a Softmax kernel that seemed
perfectly efficient, until I changed its tile shape:\nTile shape Runtime
(µs) Reuse (%) 32 × 4 115 62 8 × 16 68 89 The math didn’t change, the
memory pattern did. By aligning the tile shape better with the
hardware’s cache lines and vector units, we improved reuse and cut
runtime by over 40%.\nIt wasn’t the math - it was the layout.\n6. Why
Compilers Care Compilers don’t “see” neurons - they see loops and tiles.
They use cost models to score layouts by reuse, footprint, and schedule
efficiency. When the score changes, so does the generated code.\nIn
practice, cost models try to answer:\nHow many times will this tile be
reused before eviction? Will this layout enable vectorization or
warp-friendly access? Can we fuse downstream ops without blowing
register pressure? Layout is the bridge between algorithm and
architecture - and compilers are the translators.\n7. Closing Thoughts
Tiling isn’t just an optimization; it’s the compiler’s way of speaking
to memory. Every layer or abstraction in the ML Stack: from
TensorFlow/PyTorch to XLA/Triton to LLVM, is trying to get that layout
right.\nLayout is architecture’s accent. Every tensor speaks it;
compilers just translate.\nStay tuned: keep your friends close and your
layouts
